title: One Unbroken Line
blurb: Trace three rangoli designs without lifting your finger, then colour them in.
fact: A rangoli pattern is made of unbroken lines, which is thought to stop evil spirits from slipping in through the gaps. That's why your line couldn't break.
credit: Source: Rangoli (ICH-058), Intangible Cultural Heritage inventory, Roots.sg, National Heritage Board. Text and art are original. Background music is an original synthesized Indian-inspired instrumental.

content.prompt: Trace every line once. Lift your finger and the line breaks.

powders.name: Turmeric
powders.label: Yellow · Turmeric
powders.description: Turmeric is a yellow spice powder. Here it gives your rangoli its golden yellow colour.

powders.name: Vermilion
powders.label: Red · Vermilion
powders.description: Vermilion is a bright red pigment, represented here by the red colour.

powders.name: Flower petals
powders.label: Pink · Flower petals
powders.description: Petals are the colourful parts of flowers. Here they are represented by pink.

powders.name: Pulses
powders.label: Green · Pulses
powders.description: Pulses are dried lentils, peas and beans. Here they are represented by green.

powders.name: Rice flour
powders.label: White · Rice flour
powders.description: Rice flour is finely ground rice, represented here by white.

patterns.name: Diya
patterns.note: Some families place diyas (oil lamps) inside the rangoli and light them for a puja (prayer). Rangoli is especially prominent during Deepavali.

patterns.name: Eight-point star
patterns.note: Designs range from geometric shapes to peacock motifs, flowers and the faces of Hindu gods. Some are drawn freehand in rice flour.

patterns.name: Lotus
patterns.note: The lotus, with Goddess Lakshmi in the middle, stands for prosperity and fertility in Hinduism.

figures.caption: A large rangoli with peacock motifs, ringed by trays of coloured materials. Photo: Ms Vijayalakshmi Mohan, from Rangoli (ICH-058), Roots.sg.

figures.caption: Ms Vijayalakshmi Mohan outlines her pattern in white first, then fills the spaces inside with coloured powders, just like this game. Photo: Rangoli (ICH-058), Roots.sg.

figures.caption: Singapore-based artist Ms Vijayalakshmi Mohan with one of her rangoli. They're often drawn outside the home to bring good luck. Photo: Rangoli (ICH-058), Roots.sg.

cards.title: An array of colours
cards.text: Rangoli means ‘an array of colours’ in Sanskrit, and it's known as kolam in Tamil. The art dates back some 5,000 years and was brought to Singapore by Indian migrants.

cards.title: Drawn at the doorway
cards.text: Rangoli stands for wealth, joy and prosperity, and thanks to the deities. Drawn at the main entrance, it's believed to stop evil forces coming in, so some homes draw a fresh one every day. It's prominent at Deepavali.

cards.title: Unbroken lines
cards.text: A rangoli pattern is made of unbroken lines, thought to keep evil spirits from slipping in through the gaps. Circular designs signify the endlessness of time, and the lotus with Goddess Lakshmi stands for prosperity.

cards.title: Rice flour to recyclables
cards.text: Traditional rangoli is drawn freehand in rice flour, or filled in through a stencil. Colours come from grains, seeds, pulses, vermillion, turmeric and petals. Ms Mohan's ‘SingaRangoli’ uses 30 to 40 materials, even recyclables.

cards.title: A world record
cards.text: In 2003 Ms Mohan made a 256-square-metre rangoli at Whampoa Community Club, then the world's largest, according to the Guinness Book of Records. In 2017, 1,000 participants helped her make 1,500 ‘lantern rangoli’ for Gardens by the Bay.
